name: Rosa Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Rosa. I'm a researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, parties or government. Nothing you say will be traced back to you. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new claims team at the rural benefits office in Hollin Vale. Most applications come in online now, so I check them, ring people for missing bits, and set the claim up for a decision. I'm 27, ten months in, and I still miss things a more experienced person would spot, like a second bank account. A lot of our claimants are farm workers and older people who hate filling in forms on a screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you get on with the screen side yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it, honestly. I use AI every day, on my own phone and laptop, never with claimant details. I used it to set up online ordering for my parents' farm shop last winter, and their egg box orders doubled. I live with my partner Daniel, he's a herdsman on the Pritchard dairy farm. Between the rent on our cottage and his van, we've less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be a tool, not a miracle. At work I'd say let's use the bits that help. I'd share something on the farm shop page about how we still do things by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the job's safe, which I'm glad of, but it's not exciting. I'd still be the junior missing bank accounts. And money's tight anyway, Daniel's hours depend on the farm and milk prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, and keep using AI for the shop on the side. I'd ask my manager, Gwen, if I could help write the plain-English guides for claimants. I'd try to save 40 a month from the shop money Mum gives me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content enough. A bit bored by the idea, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Daniel's hours depend on milk prices. How does that feel at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worrying, some months. Last spring the price dropped and the Pritchards cut him to five days. We managed because of the shop money, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think about you working for the benefits office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's a bit funny about it. My dad (who's never claimed a penny in his life) says he's proud I help people, but he'd rather I helped people find work than claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, if we're smart about it. At work I'd volunteer to help bring the new systems in. On the shop page I'd post about how we're using it to save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my current job shrinks for sure, because checking online forms is exactly what AI does. But I already use these tools more than anyone in the office. I'd hope to become the person who helps older claimants use the new system, since they'll struggle. If not, the farm shop could grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gwen to put me on any pilot. I'd use AI to grow the farm shop's online orders and maybe add a delivery round to the villages. And I'd start a short online course in small business accounts, so I'm ready to take over the shop's books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. A bit nervous for the older ones in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat, who's 61 and does everything on paper first. My colleague Pat would struggle, and she's two years from her pension. I'd offer to sit with her and show her, though she might not want help from the youngest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farm shop could grow. Is that a real backup or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real, it's already making money. If AI handles the ordering and stock at the farm shop, one person could run twice the business. I could be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's very fast, and families need to look after each other. At work I'd say get ready. On the shop page I'd keep quiet, because customers don't want to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the office job's gone by 2029, there's nothing hands-on in it. The shop might hold up, because people still want to buy from a person they know. But Daniel's dairy already has a robot milker on the next farm, so his job could go around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the office before they push me, maybe within a year, and go full time at the shop with Mum and Dad. I'd use AI to run the online side and the books. Daniel and I would put off getting married until we knew where we stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd have something to do. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave the office before being pushed. Isn't that a big risk with less than a month saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but waiting is a bigger one. If I go early, I can build the shop up before everyone else in the valley starts selling eggs online. If I wait, I'm just one more person on our claims list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel about the robot milker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Daniel to learn to run the robot milker, not fight it. He knows cows better than any machine. Someone has to look after the herd when the robot breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so use it. At work I'd tell the younger ones to learn the tools now. At chapel I'd say the same to the parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do well with five years. I'd stay at the office two or three years, save, and grow the shop on the side. Then I'd go full time before 2031, with the shop already big enough to pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my AI skills into the shop now: online orders, delivery routes, the accounts. I'd save what I could from both jobs, maybe 80 a month. And I'd help Daniel learn the robot milking systems, so he's the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. A little nervous, but I like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry that a bigger shop might need robots too, by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for packing eggs. But people come to us because Mum knows their names. A robot can pack eggs, but it can't ask after your grandson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about you leaving the government job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be pleased, I think. He's always wanted me in the family business. He'd say that's where real work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone who wants to work. At chapel I'd say families should plan together. At work I'd keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 37, running the farm shop, maybe with a second one in the market town. Daniel would be running the robot milking at the Pritchards'. Ten years is a whole business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the office four or five years and get good at it, and build the shop on the side. Daniel and I would marry in the next couple of years and maybe have children. I'd invest some savings in a proper cold room for the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Like I can see the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Milk prices, Daniel's back, a bad winter. Ordinary farming things, not AI things. Those worry me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want young people in Hollin Vale to hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, but stay close to family and land. The internet can sell your eggs, but it can't raise your chickens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, mainly for Daniel and my parents. I'd land on my feet at the shop, but if the dairy goes robotic in 2031, we lose his wage. What would help is support for small family businesses to take on local workers, and training for farm workers on the new machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how rural people manage. Everyone thinks AI is a city thing. Out here it's robot milkers and online forms, and the people stuck in the middle are farm workers who've never used either.

headlineQuote: Out here it's robot milkers and online forms, and the people stuck in the middle are farm workers who've never used either.
portrait: Rosa, 27, checks **online claims** in rural Hollin Vale and still misses details.
She lives with Daniel, a **dairy herdsman**, with under a month saved.
Traditional and family-minded, she uses AI daily, including for her **parents' farm shop**.
She'd leave the office early for the **family business** if AGI came fast.
Her biggest fear is **robot milkers** taking Daniel's job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mainly because Daniel's dairy job could go by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **family businesses** to hire locally, and **training** for farm workers.
